title: Agile Estimating and Planning: Treat Every Estimate as a Conversation
summary: Mike Cohn's most useful planning ideas: story points for size, velocity for dates, planning poker to surface hidden assumptions, and why ideal days aren't calendar days.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: Agile Estimating and Planning
book.note: This article is a personal reflection from the book, focused on ideas that help software teams estimate and plan more honestly. It is not a chapter-by-chapter summary.

html:
Sprint planning, story number six. Someone asks, "How big is this one?" The developer who wrote the API last year says 3. The tester remembers that exports break on large accounts and says 13. The Product Owner glances at the sprint board and hopes for 5. A number that was supposed to describe one story is now carrying a forecast, a worry and a deadline all at once.

Mike Cohn wrote Agile Estimating and Planning for exactly that moment. The book is from 2005, and most of it still holds up because it never promises to make software predictable. It gives a team a shared way to talk about size, risk and what nobody knows yet, then lets real data turn that talk into dates.

About the book

Agile Estimating and Planning by Mike Cohn, Prentice Hall, 2005. This post picks the ideas that help most in a normal sprint planning and names the chapter each one comes from. It skips large parts of the book, including financial prioritization and the multi-team chapter. The full table of contents is on the publisher's page.

The planning matters more than the plan

Chapter 1, "The Purpose of Planning", opens with a line from the Prussian field marshal Helmuth von Moltke: "Planning is everything. Plans are nothing." Cohn builds on it a few pages later: "Agile planning shifts the emphasis from the plan to the planning," and an agile plan is one "we are not only willing, but also eager to change" (Chapter 1 excerpt, InformIT).

The same chapter explains why early numbers deserve that humility. Cohn walks through the cone of uncertainty: at the feasibility stage, a schedule estimate is typically off by 60% to 160%, so a project estimated at 20 weeks could land anywhere from 12 to 32 weeks (InformIT excerpt). That's a normal property of early work. Nobody did anything wrong.

Chapter 2, "Why Planning Fails", names the trap most teams fall into: estimates become commitments. Someone guesses eight days in January, and by March people treat that guess as a signed contract. The fix Cohn proposes is boring in a good way. Keep planning as a habit that runs through the whole project, and replan whenever the team learns something.

Here's what that looks like on a real story. Say your team needs to sync users from an old identity system. Before anyone opens the code it looks small: call one API, map a few fields, done. Then a one-day spike shows the API behaves differently per tenant, the error messages are inconsistent and test accounts are painful to create. The story didn't grow because someone was careless. The team simply knows more now.

A good replan can be tiny. Keep the original story, and split out a spike that documents tenant behavior, a read-only sync slice and a write-back slice with error handling. The question in the room moves from "why did the estimate grow?" to "which assumption changed, and which slice teaches us the most next?"

Estimate size first, let velocity do the calendar

Chapter 22 lists the reasons agile planning works, and one of them is the heading "Estimates of Size and Duration Are Separated". That idea runs through the whole book. You estimate how big something is in story points (Chapter 4). You find out how long it takes from velocity, the points your team actually finishes per iteration.

Cohn's own guide is clear that a point covers more than raw complexity: "Story points estimate total effort to complete a product backlog item," which includes the amount of work, the risk and the uncertainty. His short version is a good one to tape to the wall: "Use story points to estimate relative effort. Use velocity to forecast." (Mountain Goat Software, story points guide)

Relative sizing is easier than it sounds. A login story and a profile-edit story both sound small. But if login also touches rate limiting, password reset, audit logs and sessions on several devices, it's clearly bigger. You don't need to know the hours. You only need to answer "is this about the same as that 3-point story we did last month, or two to three times heavier?"

Keeping the two apart also lets errors cancel out over time. If your team sizes every story a bit too small, velocity comes out a bit low, and the forecast built on velocity still lands in the right place. Chapter 7, "Re-Estimating", leans on this: you don't re-estimate a story just because it took longer than hoped. You re-estimate when its size relative to other stories turns out to be wrong.

What people sayWhat it hidesA better thing to say
"This is two days."Assumes zero interruptions, zero discovery and the context of one specific person."It's like the 3-point export story, but the test setup is harder."
"Our velocity has to hit 40."Treats a measurement as a target."The last three iterations were 28, 31 and 30. Let's plan around that range."
"Split it into UI, API and DB."Produces tasks nobody can accept on their own. Chapter 12 says outright: don't split a story into tasks."What's the smallest slice a user or the PO could try and accept?"
"One ideal day is one day."Ignores meetings, reviews, support, incidents and context switching."How much focused effort is this, and how much focused time do we really have?"

Planning poker pays off in the gap between cards

Chapter 6, "Techniques for Estimating", is where planning poker shows up, under the headings "Estimates Are Shared" and "Why Planning Poker Works". The mechanics are short. The PO reads a story and answers questions. Everyone picks a card in private. All cards flip at once. If they differ, the high and low estimators explain their thinking, the team talks, and everyone votes again. Cohn notes that "usually one to three rounds is enough" (Mountain Goat Software, Planning Poker).

The private pick matters more than it looks. It stops anchoring, where the first number spoken pulls everyone toward it. It also gives the newest person on the team the same voice as the tech lead for a few seconds. And when the cards don't match, Cohn advises against averaging, because "the average hides the disagreement" (same page).

Back to the export story from the opening: "As a user, I can export my transaction history." The 3 came from someone picturing a CSV built from a query that already exists. The 13 came from someone who knows the export needs permission checks, files too big for one request, time zones, masked personal data and an audit event. Neither person was wrong. They were estimating two different stories, and the cards made that visible in under a minute.

One warning: planning poker is a bad place for a design meeting. A few minutes of questions are healthy. If the third round still splits the room, the story is probably too vague or too big. Cohn's page suggests the same: more rounds usually mean the item needs clarifying, splitting or a decision from the PO. Park it, run a spike, and move to the next card.

Ideal days, and the football game that runs three hours

Chapter 5, "Estimating in Ideal Days", opens with a question about American football. A game is sixty minutes long: four quarters of fifteen. Yet a game you watch on TV takes around three hours. The sixty minutes are ideal time. The three hours are elapsed time, full of timeouts, ads and replays.

Ideal days work the same way. "Two ideal days" means two days of focused work with nothing in the way. Real days include code review, a support question from another team, a deploy check, standup and helping a teammate with a flaky test. None of that shows up in the estimate, and all of it is real work.

So ideal days are fine as long as nobody converts them into calendar days on the way to a slide deck. The danger is that they look like calendar days, and stakeholders will read them that way. In Chapter 8, "Choosing between Story Points and Ideal Days", Cohn weighs both and leans toward story points, partly because a point can't be mistaken for a date.

Testing-heavy stories show this best. The code might be one ideal day. The team still needs test data, acceptance examples, a regression run and maybe a chat with support. Leave those out and the plan looks great on paper and stressful in real life.

Velocity belongs to the team that measured it

Another heading in Chapter 22 is "Tracking Is at the Team Level". A velocity number only makes sense inside the team that produced it, with its codebase, domain, people, interruptions and definition of done. Cohn puts it bluntly in a later article: "Story points are not a universal unit of measure," and a team with a velocity of 60 "is not necessarily twice as fast as a team with a velocity of 30" (Don't Compare Team Velocities).

The same article explains what happens when velocity turns into a score: "If velocity becomes the target, teams will get better at velocity. That does not mean they will get better at delivering value." Nobody has to cheat. Estimates drift up a little, people stop splitting big stories, and the chart looks great while the product barely moves.

Two habits keep the number honest. Count a story only when it's done, tested and accepted, so a story that's 90% coded counts as zero until a user can actually use it. And keep velocity at the team level when you plan. Pairing on a nasty bug, reviewing carefully and unblocking QA all lower one person's visible output while raising the team's. A planning number that punishes that behavior is measuring the wrong thing.

Try this sentence in planning

Swap "We commit to all 50 points" for: "Based on the last three iterations we're planning around 28 to 32 points. These two stories are risky. If they grow, this lower-priority story is the first one we move out."

If you want to see how these numbers feed a release plan with buffers and burndowns, the sibling post on agile release planning picks up from here, with Chapters 13 to 19 of the same book.

Where to start with your team

You don't need to adopt the whole book. Three small moves cover most of the value.

First, pick reference stories. Choose four the whole team remembers: a tiny bug fix, a normal CRUD change, a cross-service integration and one story that needed real discovery. Agree on their points and pin them somewhere visible. From then on, every estimate starts with "which reference is this closest to?"

Second, write the assumptions next to the number. "5 points, assuming the vendor sandbox works" is a far more useful estimate than "5". When the sandbox turns out to be down for a week, everyone can see why the plan moved, and nobody needs to defend the original guess.

Third, plan with a range once you have data. One iteration is noise. After three or four, the spread of your velocity tells you something real about what fits in a release. The aim is to make release conversations rely on evidence instead of memory and pressure. Pushing the number up is a different goal, and it breaks the number.

Try this sprint

  • Pick four reference stories with the team and agree on their points.
  • In planning poker, ask the highest and lowest card to explain before anyone votes again.
  • Write one assumption next to each estimate on the board.
  • Quote velocity as a range from your last three iterations, never as a target.
  • When a story blows up, ask which assumption changed before asking who estimated it.

Cohn's book won't make the future behave. What it gives you is a way to say "here's what we know, here's what we're guessing, and here's what we'll do if the guess is wrong" in a form that a PO, a tester and a stakeholder can all follow. That sentence alone makes most planning meetings shorter and kinder.

faqs.q: What is the difference between story points and ideal days?
faqs.a: Story points size a backlog item relative to other items and include effort, risk and uncertainty. Ideal days count focused work with no interruptions. Mike Cohn compares both in Chapter 8 of Agile Estimating and Planning and leans toward story points, partly because people tend to read ideal days as calendar days.

faqs.q: Why shouldn't an estimate be treated as a promise?
faqs.a: Early estimates carry a lot of uncertainty. Cohn cites the cone of uncertainty, where a feasibility-stage schedule estimate is typically off by 60% to 160%. Chapter 2 of his book names estimates becoming commitments as one reason planning fails. Keep the assumptions next to the number and replan when they change.

The Product Owner reads a story and answers questions, everyone picks a card privately, and all cards are revealed together. If they differ, the highest and lowest estimators explain, the team talks and votes again. One to three rounds is usually enough, and Cohn advises against averaging because it hides the disagreement.

faqs.q: Can we compare velocity between teams?
faqs.a: No. Story points mean different things on different teams, so a velocity of 60 isn't necessarily twice as fast as 30. When velocity becomes a target, teams get better at the number instead of at delivering value. Use it inside one team to forecast.
